Content:
In this topic, we’ll learn to recognize a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle from side ratios alone and use this to compute lengths quickly.

Content:
This pattern appears in some problems involving right triangles and rectangles. So, spotting it instantly can turn a multi-step geometry problem into a simple arithmetic task.

Content:
Let's refer to our standard [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/12284134d4baf55372dd5d16587aeb3c]

Content:
Notice the following:

Content:
- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 2:1]
- The ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} =\sqrt{3}:1]
- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Content:
These ratios are true for any [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. But the converse is also true:

Content:
> If at least one of these ratios is true in a right triangle, then this is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Content:
Let's see how we can use this to recognize [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangles.

sections.normalized_html:
Let's refer to our standard [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Notice the following:

  • The ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg: [MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 2:1]

  • The ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg: [MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} =\sqrt{3}:1]

  • The ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg: [MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

These ratios are true for any [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. But the converse is also true: if at least one of these ratios is true in a right triangle, then this is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

With that in mind, let's examine our right triangles in turn.

  • Triangle I is not a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Here, the ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg is the following: [MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 12\sqrt{2}:12 = \sqrt{2}:1 \neq 2:1 \quad {\color{red}\times}]

  • Triangle II is not a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Here, the ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg is the following: [MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} = 16:9 \neq \sqrt{3}:1 \quad {\color{red}\times}]

  • Triangle III is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Indeed, the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is the following: [MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 10:5\sqrt{3} = 2:\sqrt{3} \quad {\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}]

Therefore, the triangle [MATH: \textrm{III}] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Content:
Now, suppose that the diagonal of a rectangle is twice the length of its shortest side, and the area of the rectangle is [MATH: 10\sqrt{3}] square inches. Let's use this information to find the length of the shortest side of the rectangle.

Content:
First, let [MATH: s] be the length of the shortest side. Then, we have the following diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c8334834e7bf4483985c78a77855898]

Content:
Here, in rectangle [MATH: ABCD,] the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC}] is twice the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC}{:}]
[MATH: {AC}:{BC} = 2:1]

Content:
Next, since in the right triangle [MATH: ABC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg is
[MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{shortest}} = \dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{2}{1},]
we have that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d612c5b0ce8cc8520738350f4b620a9e]

Content:
Recall that the area of a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shortest side has length [MATH: s] is given by
[MATH: A = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} s^2.]

Content:
The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle, and since we're told that the area of the rectangle is [MATH: 10\sqrt 3] square inches, we have
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 10\sqrt{3} = 5\sqrt{3}.]

Content:
Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}]
[MATH: (sqrt(3))/(2)s^{2}|= 5sqrt(3); sqrt(3)s^{2}|= 10sqrt(3); s^{2}|= 10; s|= sqrt(10)]

Content:
Therefore, the shortest side of the rectangle is
[MATH: BC = s= \sqrt{10} \: \text{in}.]

sections.normalized_html: The ratio between the longest side of a rectangle and its diagonal is [MATH: \sqrt{3}:2,] and the area of the rectangle is [MATH: 108\sqrt{3}] square inches. What is the length, in inches, of the shortest side of the rectangle?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: s] be the length of the shortest side. Then, we have the following diagram.

Here, in rectangle [MATH: ABCD,]

  • the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC}] is [MATH: 2] times the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC},] and

  • the length of the longest side [MATH: \overline{AB}] is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC}.]

Thus, we have: [MATH: {AC}:{AB} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Now, since in the right triangle [MATH: ABC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is [MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{longest}} = \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}},] we have that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Recall that the area of a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shortest side has length [MATH: s] is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} s^2.]

The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle: [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 108\sqrt{3} = 54\sqrt{3}]

Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}] [MATH: (sqrt(3))/(2)s^{2}|= 54sqrt(3); sqrt(3)s^{2}|= 108sqrt(3); s^{2}|= 108; s|= sqrt(108); = sqrt(36 ⋅ 3); = 6sqrt(3)]

Therefore, the shortest side of the rectangle is [MATH: BC = s= 6\sqrt{3} \: \text{in}.]

Thus, we have: [MATH: {AC}:{AD} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Now, since in the right triangle [MATH: ADC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is [MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{longest}} = \dfrac{AC}{AD} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}},] we have that [MATH: \triangle ADC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Recall that the area of a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shortest side has length [MATH: s] is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} s^2.]

The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle: [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 200\sqrt{3} = 100\sqrt{3}]

Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}] [MATH: (sqrt(3))/(2)s^{2}|= 100sqrt(3); sqrt(3)s^{2}|= 200sqrt(3); s^{2}|= 200; s|= sqrt(200); = sqrt(100 ⋅ 2); = 10sqrt(2)]

So, the diagonal of the rectangle is [MATH: AC|= 2s; = 2 ⋅ 10sqrt(2); = 20sqrt(2).]

Finally, since the diameter of the circle is equal to the diagonal of the rectangle, we have that the diameter is [MATH: AC = 20\sqrt{2} \: \text{m}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we’ll learn to recognize a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle from side ratios alone and use this to compute lengths quickly.

Content:
This pattern appears in some problems involving right triangles and rectangles. So, spotting it instantly can turn a multi-step geometry problem into a simple arithmetic task.

Content:
Let's refer to our standard [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/12284134d4baf55372dd5d16587aeb3c]

Content:
Notice the following:

Content:
- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 2:1]
- The ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} =\sqrt{3}:1]
- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Content:
These ratios are true for any [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. But the converse is also true:

Content:
> If at least one of these ratios is true in a right triangle, then this is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Content:
Let's see how we can use this to recognize [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangles.

---

Item 2 — Example: Recognizing 30-60-90 Triangles

Example Prompt:
Consider the right triangles above (not drawn to scale). Which of the above is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle?

[IMG: /graphics/3fdf0c838e7a5e772092dcbac4f2ff01]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's refer to our standard [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/7a75a047979717f9dca94cf679a0898a]

Notice the following:

- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 2:1]
- The ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg:
[MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} =\sqrt{3}:1]
- The ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

These ratios are true for any [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. But the converse is also true: if at least one of these ratios is true in a right triangle, then this is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

With that in mind, let's examine our right triangles in turn.

- Triangle I is not a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Here, the ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg is the following:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{shortest} = 12\sqrt{2}:12 = \sqrt{2}:1 \neq 2:1 \quad {\color{red}\times}]
- Triangle II is not a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Here, the ratio of the longest leg to the shortest leg is the following:
[MATH: \text{longest} : \text{shortest} = 16:9 \neq \sqrt{3}:1 \quad {\color{red}\times}]
- Triangle III is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle. Indeed, the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is the following:
[MATH: \text{hypotenuse} : \text{longest} = 10:5\sqrt{3} = 2:\sqrt{3} \quad {\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}]

Therefore, the triangle [MATH: \textrm{III}] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Recognizing 30-60-90 Triangles in Rectangles

Content:
Now, suppose that the diagonal of a rectangle is twice the length of its shortest side, and the area of the rectangle is [MATH: 10\sqrt{3}] square inches. Let's use this information to find the length of the shortest side of the rectangle.

Content:
First, let [MATH: s] be the length of the shortest side. Then, we have the following diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c8334834e7bf4483985c78a77855898]

Content:
Here, in rectangle [MATH: ABCD,] the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC}] is twice the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC}{:}]
[MATH: {AC}:{BC} = 2:1]

Content:
Next, since in the right triangle [MATH: ABC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest leg is
[MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{shortest}} = \dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{2}{1},]
we have that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d612c5b0ce8cc8520738350f4b620a9e]

Content:
Recall that the area of a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shortest side has length [MATH: s] is given by
[MATH: A = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} s^2.]

Content:
The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle, and since we're told that the area of the rectangle is [MATH: 10\sqrt 3] square inches, we have
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 10\sqrt{3} = 5\sqrt{3}.]

Content:
Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}]
[MATH: (sqrt(3))/(2)s^{2}|= 5sqrt(3); sqrt(3)s^{2}|= 10sqrt(3); s^{2}|= 10; s|= sqrt(10)]

Content:
Therefore, the shortest side of the rectangle is
[MATH: BC = s= \sqrt{10} \: \text{in}.]

EXPLANATION

Let [MATH: s] be the length of the shortest side. Then, we have the following diagram.

Thus, we have:
[MATH: {AC}:{AB} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Now, since in the right triangle [MATH: ABC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is
[MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{longest}} = \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}},]
we have that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle:

Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}]

[MATH: BC = s= 6\sqrt{3} \: \text{in}.]
